h1: Selling brewing equipment and ingredients in India
title: Selling Brewing Kit and Ingredients | Craft Beer School
desc: How suppliers of brewing equipment, malt, hops, yeast and packaging can sell in India: customers, routes to market, import steps and service.
teaser: Indian breweries buy kit and ingredients. Selling to them takes more than a price list.
standfirst: If you make equipment or ingredients for brewers, India has buyers. This guide covers who they are, how to reach them and what the import side involves.
sections:
Buyers fall into groups. Established breweries need ingredients on a steady schedule and parts for existing plant. New breweries and brewpubs buy a full plant once and then ingredients for life. Distilleries, wineries and cideries buy some of the same items: tanks, pumps, filters and packaging. Homebrewers and small operators buy in small quantities.

Each group buys differently. An established brewery cares about reliability and delivery. A new brewery cares about advice and a price it can fund. Know which group you aim at.

Selling equipment or ingredients into India means bringing goods across the border. Central customs duty and import registration apply. The importer of record carries responsibility. Rules, duty rates and documentation change, so work with a customs broker and an adviser. We do not quote rates.

Many suppliers work through an Indian distributor or agent who handles import, stock and local sales. Others set up a subsidiary. Weigh the options with your lawyers and accountants.

Ingredients such as malt, hops and yeast are agricultural products. Rules on food safety, plant health or storage may apply. Check them early. Hops and yeast also need cold storage. A shipment left on a warm dock can lose its value.

Service counts. A brewery with a broken pump cannot wait six weeks. Buyers ask who can come to the site, how fast spare parts arrive and whether manuals and training are available in English. A local technician or a stocked distributor is a strong selling point.

Price matters. So does finance. New breweries often fund plant in stages. Payment terms that fit a build schedule can win a sale. Local manufacturers also compete, so show a clear reason to pay for imported equipment: quality, efficiency, service or a feature that others lack.

Ingredient buyers care about freshness and consistency. Ask yourself how you will get fresh hops to a brewery in a hot climate and how you will prove the malt specification.

Trade fairs, industry associations and brewing training bodies bring suppliers and brewers together. A visible presence in the brewing community builds trust. Technical talks and trial offers help new buyers test an unfamiliar product.

Content works too. Brewers search for answers about yeast, water and cleaning. A supplier who answers these well earns attention. See our note on pricing beer for retail shelves to understand what a brewery's margins look like. Read funding a brewery for how buyers pay for kit.

Choose one or two segments and one or two regions to begin. Find an agent or distributor you can trust and visit customers yourself. Build a stock plan that matches lead times. Keep the first year modest and learn.

Our guide on cash flow forecasts for a new brewery helps you see the buyer's side of a purchase.

We help equipment and ingredient suppliers from abroad enter India: defining target buyers, testing demand with brewers, preparing technical material, finding agents and distributors and planning after-sales support. Work runs remotely by video call and shared data, with site visits by arrangement.

We are not customs brokers or lawyers and we work alongside them. We do not guarantee sales or name clients.
After-sales service as a selling point

Equipment buyers worry about what happens after installation. Offer a clear plan: who commissions the plant, who trains the brewers, how spare parts reach the site and how a fault is reported and fixed. Written plans reassure more than promises.

Consider keeping a small stock of wear parts in India. A seal or a gasket available the next day matters more to a brewer than a discount on the original price.

For ingredients, offer samples and technical sheets in clear English. Brewers like to trial a new malt or hop on a small batch before they commit.

Finally, learn how your buyers plan. Breweries order ingredients around brewing schedules and busy seasons. New plants order equipment around a building timeline. If you can fit your delivery to their calendar, you become easier to buy from.
faqs: Do I need an Indian distributor?
Many suppliers use one for import, stock and service. A subsidiary is another route. Take legal and tax advice before you choose.
Do duty and import rules change?
Yes. Check current rules with a customs broker before you quote a price.
How do I prove value against local equipment?
Show reliability, efficiency data, service plans and references from brewers who use your kit.
